report:
Conclusion: the claim is **partly supported but overstated**. Vegetarian patterns are linked in some large cohorts to lower cardiovascular mortality, but evidence does **not** prove that simply avoiding meat increases life expectancy.

In Adventist Health Study 2, vegetarians had lower all-cause mortality than nonvegetarians (adjusted HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.80–0.97), but this was observational and in a generally health-conscious population: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4191896/. EPIC-Oxford found vegetarians/vegans had lower ischaemic heart disease than meat eaters, yet higher haemorrhagic and total stroke—so benefits are outcome-specific: https://www.bmj.com/content/366/bmj.l4897. A meta-analysis reported reduced ischaemic-heart-disease mortality but **no effect on all-cause or cerebrovascular mortality**: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34611632/. Diet quality also matters: healthful plant-based patterns differ from unhealthful ones in mortality risk: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34379193/.

Best interpretation: replacing processed/red meat with whole plant foods may improve cardiovascular risk and could modestly lower mortality, but “vegetarian = longer life” is not established causally; smoking, alcohol, exercise, BMI, income, food quality, and reverse causation remain major confounders.
